narrative.summary: Belgium had not yet passed a law implementing the EU AI Act or designated its authorities by October 2026; the government announced a bill for 2026 and the telecoms regulator BIPT is preparing to act as market surveillance authority, while the AI Act applies directly through the EU layer. At federal level, AI governance rests on the 2022 National Convergence Plan for AI and a 2025 federal charter for responsible AI use in public services signed by the minister and the heads of the federal administrations; the 2018 data protection law limits solely automated decisions in law enforcement, a 2022 labour law covers algorithmic management of platform workers, and a 2026 royal decree gives binding force to AI rules for real estate agents. The Data Protection Authority has issued AI guidance for professionals and citizens and ruled on automated decisions under Article 22 GDPR, and the FSMA issued a 2026 communication on frontier AI and cyber risk. Flanders has AI principles and generative AI rules for its administration and an AI-in-education vision, Wallonia's 2025–2029 digital strategy has an AI priority, and Brussels has a generative AI good-practice guide. Several bills on deepfakes, AI in public administration and biometric identification are pending.

instruments.english_title: Act of 30 July 2018 on the protection of natural persons with regard to the processing of personal data
instruments.issuing_authority: Federal Parliament (Chamber of Representatives) and the King (Federal Government of Belgium)
instruments.current_status: In force. Law of 30 July 2018 (Dutch title: 'Wet betreffende de bescherming van natuurlijke personen met betrekking tot de verwerking van persoonsgegevens'), published in the Moniteur belge on 5 September 2018 (NUMAC 2018040581, p. 68616), entry into force 5 September 2018 per the Justel header; amended several times since (consolidated version on Justel). It is the national GDPR implementing law and transposes the Law Enforcement Directive (EU) 2016/680 in Title 2. No amendment referring to artificial intelligence was identified.
instruments.scope: Belgium (federal); processing of personal data by public and private controllers, with specific regimes for criminal-justice authorities (Title 2) and intelligence and security services (Title 3)
instruments.summary: Belgium's framework data protection law implementing the GDPR and transposing the Law Enforcement Directive. Its AI-relevant provisions are in Title 2 (arts. 25-71, processing by competent authorities for the prevention, investigation and prosecution of criminal offences): article 35 allows decisions based solely on automated processing, including profiling, that produce adverse legal effects or significantly affect the person only where a law, decree, ordinance, EU law or international agreement provides appropriate safeguards, at least the right to obtain human intervention from the controller, and prohibits profiling that results in discrimination on the basis of the special categories of data in article 34.
instruments.ai_governance_relevance: Sets the national rules on automated decision-making and profiling by police and criminal-justice authorities, and the general data protection framework that governs AI training and use.

instruments.official_title: Loi portant des dispositions diverses relatives au travail
instruments.english_title: Act of 3 October 2022 containing various provisions relating to work (platform economy chapter: presumption of employment for digital platform work)
instruments.issuing_authority: Federal Parliament (Chamber of Representatives) and the King (Federal Government of Belgium)
instruments.current_status: In force. Law of 3 October 2022 (Dutch title: 'Wet houdende diverse arbeidsbepalingen'), published in the Moniteur belge on 10 November 2022 (NUMAC 2022206360, p. 81963). The law entered into force on 20 November 2022; under its article 18, section 1 of chapter 4 'Economie de plateformes' (which inserts article 337/3 into the Programme Law (I) of 27 December 2006) applies from 1 January 2023, and section 2 (accident insurance for platform workers) from a date to be set by the King. Belgium must also transpose the EU Platform Work Directive (EU) 2024/2831, including its algorithmic-management chapter, by 2 December 2026; no transposition bill had been tabled in the Chamber by 8 October 2026.
instruments.scope: Belgium (federal); work performed via digital platforms that issue orders ('plateformes numériques donneuses d'ordres')
instruments.summary: Omnibus labour law (the 2022 'labour deal') that, among other measures, introduces in article 337/3 of the Programme Law (I) of 27 December 2006 a rebuttable presumption of an employment relationship for people working through digital platforms. It defines a digital platform that issues orders as one that organises the work 'via an algorithm or any other equivalent method or technology', and requires that the qualification of the working relationship take account of the use of algorithms in the organisation of work. It is Belgium's first federal law to refer explicitly to algorithmic management of workers.
instruments.ai_governance_relevance: Explicitly links employment-status rules to algorithmic organisation of work on digital labour platforms.

instruments.issuing_authority: The King, on the proposal of the Minister for Middle Classes (Federal Government of Belgium); code drawn up by the National Council of the Professional Institute of Real Estate Agents (IPI/BIV)
instruments.current_status: Royal decree signed 20 July 2026 and published in the Moniteur belge on 21 September 2026 (NUMAC 2026006656), whose article 1 makes the annexed code of ethics binding. Article 2 repeals the royal decree of 29 June 2018 approving the previous code with effect from 1 October 2026; the decree contains no separate commencement clause.
instruments.scope: Belgium (federal); all real estate agents registered with the Professional Institute of Real Estate Agents and persons for whom they are responsible
instruments.summary: Royal decree giving binding force to the new code of ethics of Belgium's real estate agents, which adds a sub-title on the use of artificial intelligence and defines an 'AI system' in article 5 in terms aligned with the EU AI Act. Articles 43-45 provide that using an AI system cannot override an agent's ethical and legal duties; agents must critically review AI-generated output, be transparent with third parties about (even partial) AI use where legal obligations require, and have sufficient competence to control the systems used; they may not enter personal data into an 'open' AI system or use AI to deceive people.
instruments.ai_governance_relevance: One of the first federal regulatory texts setting binding professional rules on the use of AI (including generative AI tools) by a regulated profession.

instruments.english_title: Charter for the responsible use of artificial intelligence in public services in the provision of services to individuals, businesses and organisations
instruments.issuing_authority: Minister of Public Action and Modernisation, in charge of Digital Affairs (Vanessa Matz), with the Chairs of the College of Federal Public Services, the College of Public-Interest Bodies and the College of Public Social Security Institutions, on behalf of 40 adhering federal public bodies
instruments.current_status: Signed on 11 July 2025 (date on the signature page) by the Minister of Public Action and Modernisation and the chairs of the three federal colleges; Annex 2 lists the adhering federal public services, Defence, Federal Police, public-interest bodies and public social security institutions (40 bodies). It is a self-commitment of the adhering bodies, each of which must implement it in its strategic and operational policy; it creates no new legal obligations. Dutch title: 'Charter voor verantwoord gebruik van artificiële intelligentie in overheidsdiensten bij de dienstverlening aan individuen, bedrijven en organisaties'. The Minister's general policy note of 24 January 2026 (Chamber DOC 56 1282/030) states that it is to be extended to autonomous public enterprises. It follows a public consultation on a draft prepared by the AI4Belgium Ethics & Law working group in spring 2024.
instruments.scope: Adhering federal public bodies, for AI systems used to take or support administrative decisions or to interact directly with individuals, businesses and organisations
instruments.summary: Federal charter under which adhering public bodies commit to eight principles whenever they design, develop, procure or use AI systems (as defined by the EU AI Act, including generative AI) to take or support administrative decisions or to interact directly with the public: the option to deal with a staff member instead of an AI system, transparency (always telling people they are interacting with AI and documenting systems), human oversight of high-risk systems, the right of appeal, data quality, prior risk assessment and mitigation (including for purchased systems, with independent audits where appropriate), environmental sustainability and continuous AI training of staff. Bodies state they will not use an AI system that does not meet these principles, and each adhering body must build the charter into its strategic and operational policy.
instruments.ai_governance_relevance: Main federal instrument governing the use of AI by Belgian federal public administrations.

instruments.english_title: Litigation Chamber Decision 168/2023 of 19 December 2023: automated suspension of a customer account based on a credit-agency payment profile
instruments.current_status: Decision (order under the simplified procedure, Article 95 §1 of the Act of 3 December 2017) of the Litigation Chamber; appeal possible to the Market Court within 30 days of notification. Published in French; the file on the APD site is named 'bevel-nr.-168-2023.pdf'. No later appeal ruling was found in this review.
instruments.summary: On a complaint against a car-sharing platform that automatically suspended a user's account because a Dutch credit agency rated his payment profile as risky, the Litigation Chamber found that the platform had taken an automated decision falling under Article 22 GDPR as interpreted in CJEU SCHUFA (C-634/21). It ordered the platform to comply with the access and erasure requests within 30 days, including information on the logic behind the automated decision, and issued a warning on the compliance of the processing leading to automatic suspension with Articles 5, 6 and 22 GDPR (human intervention, the right to contest, a lawful basis).

instruments.english_title: Communication FSMA_2026_15 of 15 June 2026 — Impact of frontier AI systems on cyber risk
instruments.current_status: FSMA communication published 15 June 2026 in French, Dutch and English, setting out supervisory expectations addressed primarily to entities subject to DORA; the FSMA invites other financial entities to apply them.
instruments.summary: Warns firms supervised by the FSMA that frontier AI models able to find and exploit software vulnerabilities at industrial scale sharply raise cyber risk, so that even small firms must revise upwards the likelihood and impact of an attack and shorten patching cycles. It sets out measures under the DORA Regulation in four groups (identify ICT assets; protect them through scanning, patching, access control, backups and network segmentation; detect and respond to incidents; challenge ICT providers) and states that the FSMA expects all DORA entities to implement them swiftly, noting that AI can also be used defensively.
